finance-professionals-career-mobility-po.author: Tara E. Shaw, LL.B, ICD.D Candidate
finance-professionals-career-mobility-po.core: Posted in last 7 days Finance Professionals - Career Mobility Podcast Guests The consensus is in: Career mobility is shaped by embracing opportunities (maybe even more so if you are scared), the relationships you build along the way, having courage to support your viewpoint, but being open to change, and - no surprise to a room full of finance professionals - the optionality that comes from building your own financial security. Sprinkled on top, as an audience member prompted with a pointed question, our panel admitted that, sometimes, it’s also about good timing and just a little luck. These were the themes that stood out at the AFP YYC Career Mobility 2026 panel discussion that I had the opportunity to moderate. Thank you to our panelists Gloria Hartl, MBA, CRMP, ICD.D, Jon Wrathall, Sarah O'Connor, Travis Patzer, AFP YYC, our sponsors, and the engaged audience for a wonderful evening. A few other nuggets that we took away from the evening: - Success is leaving a place better than how you found it. - Never stop learning about yourself. - Do something that scares you every day (but make sure you can sleep at night with your decisions). - Enjoy the moment. (It doesn't come back.) Gloria Hartl, MBA, CRMP, ICD.Deven turned the tables on me when she asked what career advice would I give to my children. I admit, I was wholly unprepared to respond to one of my own questions! After some reflection this weekend, and nudged by a question from the wise Rebecca Regnier on success and balance, my answer today is this: Build a full life with intention, one that includes a career, be sure to fill it with everyone and everything you love, have courage and leave a little room for luck. As I write this, I’m reminded of the wise words that a former colleague wrote upon his retirement that I meant to share with the panel. It was something to the effect of - work hard, meet your (quarterly and annual) deadlines, but don’t miss your children’s basketball games or piano recitals. IYKYK. But sometimes, in the rush of a deal or deadline or emergency, that’s easier said than done! Even our wise panelists said that there were times when they had to make tough choices about where they spent their time but that ultimately they were present for the important ones with their family. Speaking of building a full life, if you enjoyed this discussion and would like to hear more like it, I’m launching a podcast with stories of intentional work, life and being. I’m exploring the work that goes into those moments before the next one takes shape. If you’d like to be a part of it, I'd love to hear from you - send me a message. #AFP YYC #associationforfinanceprofessionalscalgarychapter #careermobility #podcast #intentional #legermainhotel Zane Bahari-Robart Zoya Younis Farrah Talakshi (Panjwani), CTP, MBA Lukas Chiodo Jon Sweezey, CTP Jeffrey Stoy, CTP

scientists-in-russian-far-east-research-.core: Posted in last 7 days Scientists in Russian Far East - Research Priorities & Military Ties Russia wants to attract more scientists. But what kind of research does it actually want them to do? In September 2026, Vladimir Putin proposed a special programme to attract Russian and foreign researchers to the Russian Far East. The government was asked to consider housing, relocation allowances, and support for scientists' families. At first glance, it sounds like an initiative to develop regional science. But there's another side to this story. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the relationship between scientific research and the military-industrial complex has become an increasingly important question. Universities and research institutions are operating in a country where defense production is a major state priority, international scientific cooperation has been severely disrupted, and researchers face growing political pressures. The Russian Far East is particularly interesting in this context. The region is home to major defense manufacturers, while some local universities and research institutions already collaborate with military-industrial enterprises or work on technologies with both civilian and military applications. But does this mean the new initiative is intended to support military research? Not necessarily. And that's precisely what I'm trying to investigate. I'm currently working on an article for T-invariant, speaking with researchers and experts on Russian science policy and defense technology, examining existing university-industry partnerships, and trying to understand how scientific priorities have changed since 2022. What interests me most is not simply whether scientists will move to the Far East, but what kind of research environment awaits them. Who will determine their research priorities? How much independence will they have? And what happens to fundamental science when technological development becomes increasingly tied to state and military interests? I think these questions deserve far more attention than the promises of housing and financial incentives. More to come once the article is published. #SciencePolicy #AcademicFreedom #ScienceJournalism #Russia
